text.content: Script:

rich_text.plain_text: Script:

text.content: "That's a fair read, and I'd rather meet it head-on than dodge it. Yes — this is consulting. I'm not going to pretend it's something else. The difference is where the consultant stops and where I start. A consultant hands you a recommendation and an invoice, and then it's your problem to go build it. I diagnose what's actually breaking in your revenue engine, and then my team builds the machine that fixes it — and I stay on the number it's supposed to move. Concretely: if your reps are inconsistent, I don't write you a 'sales process playbook' — we build something like the Call Grader we run on our own team, that scores every call against what good looks like and tells a rep exactly where they lost the deal. I'm not selling you advice about that. I'm selling you the thing itself, plus the judgment to know it's the right thing to build."

text.content: Script:

rich_text.plain_text: Script:

text.content: "Honest answer — it depends where your revenue is actually leaking, and finding that is the first thing we do, before I sell you anything. There are two shapes this takes. If the problem is you're not putting enough into the top of the funnel, we build the outreach engine — automated, personalized SDR motion that fills pipeline without you hiring four reps. If the problem is you're leaking deals you already have — follow-ups that never happen, deals that go dark between call one and call two — we build something like DealForge, which generates the assets and the next-step structure that drag a stalled deal back to a close. Most companies your size are bleeding 20 to 40 percent of pipeline to leakage they can't even see. On a $2M pipeline, moving your close rate from 20 to 25 percent is $100K you already earned and were losing. But I won't tell you which machine you need until I've diagnosed the constraint. That diagnosis is the first thing you're buying — and it's the part nobody else does."

text.content: Script:

rich_text.plain_text: Script:

text.content: "Two reasons, and only one of them is maintenance — so let me give you the real one first. After we ship the first machine, I don't disappear. I stay diagnosing. Your business changes every quarter — new products, new reps, new competitors — and that continuous read keeps surfacing the next revenue gap worth building for. You might start with the Revenue Dashboard so you can finally see your pipeline, and three months in the data makes it obvious your reps need Call Grader, and a quarter after that it's clear your top of funnel is the real constraint and we build the SDR engine. The retainer is what funds an operator who keeps finding the next $100K. The second reason is the boring one: the systems you're running daily keep running and keep learning your business — stop paying and they stop evolving with you. But you're not paying me to keep the lights on. You're paying me to keep finding money."

text.content: Script:

rich_text.plain_text: Script:

text.content: "I get the reflex — 'custom' usually means blank check. It doesn't here, and there are three reasons. One: you start on a fixed three-month pilot. Known number, capped, no surprises while we prove the thing works. Two: the retainer is a flat monthly, not billed per build — you're buying throughput, not piecework, so the month I build you two machines costs the same as the month I build one. Three, and this is the part people don't expect: most of what you'll need, we've already built. You can see it — the dashboard, Call Grader, the SDR engine, DealForge — those exist. Deploying one of those is fast and predictable. Genuinely net-new custom is the exception, and when it comes up I scope it and price it before a developer touches a keyboard. You will never get an invoice for something you didn't sign off on."

text.content: Script:

rich_text.plain_text: Script:

text.content: "An agency executes a brief you write. A dev shop builds the spec you hand them. Both of them need you to already know the answer — and both get paid whether or not the thing moves your revenue. That's the whole difference. You don't bring me a spec. You bring me a revenue problem — 'my close rate is stuck,' 'my reps are inconsistent,' 'my pipeline's drying up' — and I diagnose what's actually wrong before anyone builds anything. Then I architect the fix, my team ships it — that's where something like Call Grader or DealForge comes from — and I stay accountable to the number it was supposed to move. The diagnosis and the ownership of the outcome are the parts neither an agency nor a dev shop will ever touch, because they own a deliverable. I own your result."
